body:
Energy changes form but is conserved

In everyday processes, energy often changes from one form to another. A falling stone gains kinetic energy while losing gravitational potential energy. An electric lamp converts electrical energy mainly into light and thermal energy. A moving bicycle slows when friction transfers mechanical energy into other forms, including thermal energy.

Law of conservation of energy: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed. It can be transferred or converted from one form to another, but the total energy of an isolated system remains constant.

The word isolated matters because energy may pass between an object and its surroundings. When a moving object comes to rest due to friction, its kinetic energy has not disappeared. Energy has been transferred to the object, contact surfaces and surroundings, largely as thermal energy.

Conversion between potential and kinetic energy

Consider a 2 kg object released from rest at a height of 3 m. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), and neglect air resistance. At the beginning, its speed is zero. Its kinetic energy is therefore zero, while its gravitational potential energy is:

\(E_p=mgh=2\times10\times3=60\,\mathrm{J}\)

As the object falls, its height decreases and its speed increases. Gravitational potential energy changes into kinetic energy.

  • At height 3 m: Potential energy is 60 J, kinetic energy is 0 J, and total mechanical energy is 60 J.
  • At height 1.5 m: Potential energy is 30 J, kinetic energy is 30 J, and total mechanical energy remains 60 J.
  • Just before reaching height 0 m: Potential energy is 0 J, kinetic energy is 60 J, and total mechanical energy remains 60 J.

This example illustrates the conservation of mechanical energy when energy losses to air resistance and other non-conservative effects are neglected:

$$E_{\mathrm{mechanical}}=E_p+E_k=\mathrm{constant}$$

Mechanical energy is the sum of potential and kinetic energies. If the only relevant force doing work is gravity, a decrease in gravitational potential energy produces an equal increase in kinetic energy.

A swing illustrates the same principle

A child on a swing provides another familiar example. Near the highest point of the swing's path, its speed is small and its gravitational potential energy is relatively high. As the swing moves towards its lowest point, gravitational potential energy decreases while kinetic energy increases. Near the lowest point, speed is greatest and gravitational potential energy is lowest relative to that path.

A real swing gradually slows down unless additional energy is supplied. Air resistance and friction at the support transfer some of its mechanical energy to the surroundings. Total energy is still conserved, even though the swing's mechanical energy decreases.

Energy conversions in daily life

Many ordinary processes involve more than one conversion. In a battery-operated torch, chemical energy stored in the battery supplies electrical energy, which the torch converts into light and thermal energy. In a moving bicycle, chemical energy obtained from food supports muscular action, which produces mechanical motion; some energy is also transferred as heat.

During photosynthesis, green plants convert part of the light energy received from the Sun into stored chemical energy. These examples demonstrate that different forms of energy are connected by natural and human-made processes.

Gujarat example: hydroelectric generation at Ukai

Hydroelectric generation illustrates an important conversion of mechanical energy into electrical energy. Water stored at an elevated level possesses gravitational potential energy. As the water flows downward, it gains kinetic energy, which is used to turn machinery connected to an electrical generator.

The Ukai Hydroelectric Power Station on the Tapi River in Gujarat is a practical example of this process. The Central Electricity Authority listed Ukai among Gujarat's operating hydroelectric projects in its state profile dated 18 November 2024. This dated listing establishes the project's status in that source; it is not a claim about its operating condition at every later moment.

In actual generation, not all the water's available energy becomes electrical energy. Some is transferred into other forms. This does not violate the law of conservation of energy.

Total energy and mechanical energy are not always the same

Total energy is conserved. Mechanical energy remains constant only under suitable conditions, such as ideal free fall without air resistance. When friction is present, mechanical energy may decrease because energy is converted into thermal energy or other forms.

Prelims focus

  • Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it is transferred or converted.
  • Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energies.
  • During ideal free fall, gravitational potential energy decreases while kinetic energy increases.
  • Without air resistance, the total mechanical energy of a freely falling object remains constant.
  • Friction may convert mechanical energy into thermal energy.
  • Trap: A decrease in mechanical energy does not mean that total energy has been destroyed.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 11, 'Work and Energy', Sections 11.2.5–11.2.6, printed pp. 154–155, 2018–19 text; Central Electricity Authority, 'State Profile on Hydro Development for Gujarat', table 'H.E. Projects in Operation', status dated 18 November 2024, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: During ideal free fall, potential energy decreases by exactly the amount kinetic energy increases.

title: Conservation of Energy and Conversion Between Energy Forms

body:
Why time matters

Two people may lift identical loads through the same height and therefore do the same amount of work. However, if one completes the lifting in less time, that person performs the work at a greater rate.

Power measures how quickly work is done or energy is transferred. It does not simply measure the total amount of work performed.

Power is the rate of doing work or the rate of transfer of energy.

\(P=\frac{W}{t}\)

In this expression, \(P\) denotes power, \(W\) denotes work done and \(t\) denotes the time taken. When the rate varies, dividing the total work by the total time gives the average power over that interval.

SI unit of power

The SI unit of power is the watt (W), named after James Watt.

\(1\,\mathrm{W}=1\,\mathrm{J/s}\)

A device operating at a power of 1 W transfers or converts energy at a rate of 1 J every second. Larger powers are commonly expressed in kilowatts.

\(1\,\mathrm{kW}=1000\,\mathrm{W}\)

The symbol \(W\) can represent work in an equation, while W is also the SI unit symbol for watt. The meaning depends on context: work is measured in joules, whereas power is measured in watts.

Same work, different power

Consider 2 workers who each lift a load weighing 200 N through a vertical height of 2 m. Both perform the same work against gravity:

\(W=Fs=200\times2=400\,\mathrm{J}\)

Worker 1 completes the lift in 10 s:

\(P_1=\frac{400}{10}=40\,\mathrm{W}\)

Worker 2 completes the lift in 20 s:

\(P_2=\frac{400}{20}=20\,\mathrm{W}\)

Both workers do 400 J of work, but Worker 1 develops twice the average power because the same work is completed in half the time.

Power and energy consumption

Power can also describe the rate at which an appliance uses electrical energy. A 100 W lamp operating at a constant power rating uses energy at a rate of 100 J every second. In 10 s, it uses:

\(E=Pt=100\times10=1000\,\mathrm{J}\)

More generally, for constant power during a time interval:

\(E=Pt\)

This relationship connects power and energy, but it does not make them interchangeable. A higher-power appliance may consume less total energy than a lower-power appliance if it operates for a sufficiently shorter time.

Average power when the rate changes

A person or machine may work faster during one interval and slower during another. Average power is found by dividing the total work done by the total time taken. For example, if a machine performs 600 J of work in 15 s, its average power over that interval is 40 W, regardless of whether its rate was constant throughout.

Prelims focus

  • Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy.
  • \(P=\frac{W}{t}\).
  • The SI unit of power is watt (W).
  • \(1\,\mathrm{W}=1\,\mathrm{J/s}\).
  • \(1\,\mathrm{kW}=1000\,\mathrm{W}\).
  • Trap: More power means a higher rate of energy transfer, not necessarily a greater total amount of energy used.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 11, 'Work and Energy', Section 11.3, 'Rate of Doing Work', printed pp. 155–156, 2018–19 text.]

pictures.alt: Both workers lift 200 N through 2 m and do 400 J of work; taking 10 s gives 40 W, while taking 20 s gives 20 W.
pictures.caption: Equal work can be performed at different rates.

title: Power: The Rate of Doing Work

body:
Why electrical energy is measured in kilowatt-hours

The joule is the SI unit of energy, but it is relatively small for expressing the electricity used by homes, shops and factories over many hours. Electrical energy consumption is therefore commonly expressed in kilowatt-hours (kWh).

One kilowatt-hour (1 kWh) is the energy consumed or transferred when a power of 1 kilowatt is maintained for 1 hour.

A kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy, not a unit of power. The kilowatt tells us the rate of energy use, while the hour tells us how long that rate is maintained.

Relationship between kilowatt-hour and joule

One kilowatt is 1000 W, and 1 hour is 3600 s. Since power multiplied by time gives energy:

$$\begin{aligned}1\,\mathrm{kWh}&=1000\,\mathrm{W}\times3600\,\mathrm{s}\\&=3600000\,\mathrm{J}\\&=3.6\times10^6\,\mathrm{J}\end{aligned}$$

\(\boxed{1\,\mathrm{kWh}=3.6\times10^6\,\mathrm{J}}\)

In ordinary household electricity billing in India, 1 unit of electrical energy means 1 kWh.

Calculating electrical energy consumption

For an appliance operating at constant power:

\(\mathrm{Energy\ in\ kWh}=\mathrm{Power\ in\ kW}\times\mathrm{Time\ in\ hours}\)

Before using this expression, convert a power rating given in watts into kilowatts by dividing by 1000. Convert a duration given in minutes into hours when necessary.

Example 1: An electric lamp

A 100 W lamp operates continuously for 5 hours.

Its power in kilowatts is \(100/1000=0.1\,\mathrm{kW}\).

\(E=0.1\times5=0.5\,\mathrm{kWh}\)

The lamp consumes 0.5 unit of electrical energy. In joules, this is:

\(0.5\times3.6\times10^6=1.8\times10^6\,\mathrm{J}\)

Example 2: A higher-power appliance

A 500 W appliance operates continuously for 1 hour.

\(E=0.5\times1=0.5\,\mathrm{kWh}\)

Despite its higher power rating, this appliance consumes the same amount of energy as the 100 W lamp used for 5 hours.

Example 3: A heater

A 2 kW heater operates continuously at that power for 3 hours.

\(E=2\times3=6\,\mathrm{kWh}\)

Its energy consumption is 6 units. If the heater switches off during part of that period or operates at a different power, the actual consumption must be calculated using its operating durations and powers.

Common distinctions in objective questions

Work, energy and power are closely related, but each answers a different question.

  • Work: How much energy is transferred through the action of a force and displacement? Its SI unit is joule (J).
  • Energy: How much capacity to do work is possessed or transferred? Its SI unit is also joule (J).
  • Power: How quickly is work done or energy transferred? Its SI unit is watt (W).
  • Kilowatt-hour: How much electrical energy is used over a period of time? It is a larger unit of energy equal to \(3.6\times10^6\) J.

When several appliances are used, the total electrical energy consumption is the sum of the energy consumed by each appliance. Thus, electricity consumption depends on both the power ratings of appliances and how long they operate.

Complete revision of the relationships

Force acting through displacement produces work. An object's motion gives it kinetic energy, while its height or changed shape can give it potential energy. Energy can be transferred and converted between forms, but the total energy of an isolated system is conserved. Power expresses the rate of work or energy transfer, and multiplying power by time gives the energy used.

Prelims focus

  • Kilowatt-hour (kWh) is a commercial unit of electrical energy.
  • \(1\,\mathrm{kWh}=3.6\times10^6\,\mathrm{J}\).
  • One electricity unit ordinarily represents 1 kWh.
  • Energy used at constant power equals power multiplied by operating time.
  • Power must be expressed in kW and time in hours when calculating energy directly in kWh.
  • Trap: Kilowatt (kW) measures power; kilowatt-hour (kWh) measures energy.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 11, 'Work and Energy', Section 11.3.1, 'Commercial Unit of Energy', printed pp. 156–157, 2018–19 text; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 11, Sections 11.1–11.3, printed pp. 146–157, for the concluding comparison.]

pictures.caption: Power and operating time together determine electrical energy consumption.

title: Kilowatt-Hour: The Commercial Unit of Electrical Energy
